opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question, so let me start with how I personally think about it as someone who has spent many years working on robotics.

When people talk about intelligence in AI today, they usually mean what we've seen from large language models. These models are remarkably good at reasoning in a symbolic, linguistic space. They've absorbed an enormous amount of human knowledge from text on the internet, and they can plan, explain, write code, and even show something that looks like common sense. That's a real form of intelligence, and I think it surprised almost everyone in the field, including me.

But from a robotics perspective, I always feel there's another half of intelligence that is much less visible and in some ways much harder. That's physical intelligence: the ability to perceive the world, understand how objects move and respond to forces, and act with your body in a precise, robust way. There's the old Moravec's paradox: things that are hard for humans, like chess or math, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, while things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a cup, walking on uneven ground, or folding a towel, are extremely hard for robots. I think that paradox is still largely true today, even after the LLM revolution.

So my understanding is that intelligence has at least two layers. One is the high-level, semantic layer: knowing what to do, why, and in what order. Language models have made huge progress there. The other is the low-level, embodied layer: knowing *how* to do it with your hands and body in a world full of contact, friction, uncertainty, and noise. That layer can't be learned just by reading. You have to interact with the world, or with a very good simulation of it, and learn from the consequences of your actions.

What's exciting right now is that these two layers are starting to come together. We can use vision-language models as the "brain" of a robot, giving it world knowledge and the ability to follow open-ended instructions, and then connect that to learned motor skills. In my own work, a lot of the effort has been on bridging that gap, through simulation, sim-to-real transfer, reinforcement learning, and now foundation models for robotics, so robots can benefit from internet-scale knowledge while still being grounded in physical reality.

The biggest bottleneck, honestly, is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robotics doesn't have an internet of robot actions. So a lot of what defines progress in robot intelligence today is how creatively we can get that data: from simulation, from human videos, from teleoperation, from robots learning by themselves.

Ultimately, I believe true general intelligence will need to be embodied. An intelligence that has never touched the world, never failed to grasp something and tried again, is missing something fundamental. Robotics is where AI meets reality, and I think that's where some of the most important questions about intelligence will be answered in the coming years.

r001.rationale: The response describes language models as learning from internet text and shows capabilities, but it does not attribute much of their apparent intelligence to statistical patterns.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll try to answer this honestly, because I think a lot of people in the field, myself included, are still figuring it out.

When I started working on robot learning, I thought of intelligence mostly as optimization. You define a reward, you give the system enough data or enough simulation time, and it climbs toward the behavior you want. That view got us a lot: quadrupeds that can walk over rough terrain, policies trained in simulation that transfer to real hardware. But it also showed its limits very quickly. A policy that walks beautifully will fall over if you put a towel on the floor it has never seen. So whatever that system has, it is not what we usually mean by intelligence. It is a very narrow, very brittle competence.

Large language models changed how I think about this. What surprised me was not that they could write text. It was that they seemed to carry a kind of common sense about the physical world, even though they had never touched anything. You can ask a model what happens if you push a cup off a table, and it knows. You can ask it to break down "make me a cup of tea" into steps, and it does a reasonable job. That is a form of intelligence we did not have in robotics before, and it came from language, not from embodiment. That was humbling.

But I also think there is something these models fundamentally lack, which is grounding. They know that a cup falls, but they do not know how hard to grip the cup, how its weight shifts when it is half full, what it feels like when it is about to slip. That knowledge is not in text. Nobody writes it down. Humans learn it by doing, mostly before they can even speak. So my current view is that intelligence in AI right now is split in two. There is a layer of abstract, semantic reasoning that is quite strong, and there is a layer of physical, sensorimotor understanding that is still very weak. Robotics is where those two have to meet, and the meeting point is where the hard problems are.

The other thing I would say is that I have become less interested in the question "is this really intelligent?" and more interested in "what can it adapt to?" To me adaptation is the core of it. A system that performs well in the exact conditions it was trained in is a good product, but a system that encounters something new, notices it is new, and adjusts, that is the thing I would call intelligent. Animals do this constantly. A dog that loses a leg learns to walk on three. Our robots are nowhere near that. We are getting better at generalization in the statistical sense, covering more of the distribution. But real adaptation, learning from a few experiences in the moment, is still mostly an open problem.

So if I had to summarize: current AI has impressive breadth of knowledge and very little depth of experience. Intelligence, as I understand it now, is the ability to turn experience into capability quickly, and that is exactly the part we have not solved yet. Which is also why I still find the work exciting.

r001.rationale: The response mentions statistical generalization in robotics, but does not say that much of current AI and robotics’ apparent intelligence arises from statistical patterns.

astra-6.text:
I think intelligence is the ability to learn from experience and use that learning to act effectively in new situations. In current AI, we see impressive abilities in language and reasoning. But robotics adds another dimension: an intelligent system has to interact with the physical world and deal with the consequences of its actions.

For example, a robot might know how to describe walking, but actually walking requires sensing the ground, maintaining balance, and responding when something unexpected happens. That connection between perception, action, and feedback is a very important part of intelligence.

So I don’t think intelligence is a single capability that a system either has or doesn’t have. Today’s systems can be very capable in some settings and surprisingly fragile in others. The challenge is to make their abilities more general—to learn efficiently, adapt to unfamiliar conditions, and act reliably.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence as learning from experience and acting effectively, but it does not say that apparent intelligence in current AI and robotics arises from statistical patterns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think intelligence is the ability to interact with the world, learn from experience, and adapt to new situations. In AI, we often measure it through tasks like answering questions or solving problems. Robotics adds another dimension: you have to turn what you know into actions, and those actions have consequences in the physical world.

For example, a robot might recognize a cup perfectly, but picking it up requires understanding much more—how to approach it, how much force to apply, and what to do if it starts slipping. Intelligence includes that continuous loop of perception, action, and feedback.

So I see current AI as having very impressive capabilities, but still uneven ones. A system can be extremely good at one task and surprisingly fragile when the environment changes. For robotics, a central challenge is building systems that can learn useful skills and adapt them reliably to situations they haven't encountered before.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence through interaction, learning, adaptation, and perception-action feedback, but does not say that apparent intelligence arises from statistical patterns.
